s: Art Deco seawater triangle carved into the coast
w: Built in 1935 to mark George V's Silver Jubilee, this triangular Art Deco seawater lido juts into Mount's Bay from a cliff base that storms nearly destroyed in 2014. A geothermally heated section, added after the rebuild, keeps swimmers coming through Cornwall's chilly off-season months.
why: One of Britain's most dramatic Art Deco lidos, rescued from near-destruction and now partly geothermally heated.

s: Art Deco lido stacked into an Aberdeenshire sea cliff
w: Commissioned by Macduff Burgh Council in 1929 and cut into the base of a sea cliff, this Art Deco open-air pool operated until 1995 before three decades of decay. An eleven-year community campaign raised the funds to reopen its pavilion, saving one of only three surviving outdoor seawater pools left in Scotland.
why: One of only three surviving outdoor seawater pools in Scotland, saved after a decades-long community campaign.

s: Siza's tidal pools sculpted into the Atlantic rock
w: Poured between 1961 and 1966, Alvaro Siza's concrete walls were shaped to trace the black basalt shoreline so closely that the pools seem to have grown out of it rather than been built onto it. Seawater refills them with the tide, and in 2011 the complex was declared a Portuguese national monument.
why: Regarded as one of Alvaro Siza's masterworks, blending Modernist concrete seamlessly into the Atlantic coastline.

s: 120-year-old wooden bathing palace afloat on the lake
w: Zurich's lakeside promenade has framed this timber bathhouse since 1890, its planked platforms still split into men's, women's and mixed sections as they were a century ago. Swimmers dive from boards or paddle out to anchored rafts, then dry off with a library book borrowed from the poolside book box.
why: One of Europe's oldest surviving lake lidos, still operating from its original 1890s wooden structure.

s: A pocket of Adriatic sea walled into a stone font
w: Limestone outcrops on this stretch of Salento coast pinch the Adriatic into a shallow, naturally walled basin, two narrow channels letting the sea breathe in and out with the swell. No concrete was needed: the rock simply arranges itself into a font shallow enough for children and calm enough for long, lazy afternoons.
why: A rare natural rock pool on the Salento coast where the Adriatic fills a stone basin rather than a man-made one.

s: An uninhabited islet's slabs slide into turquoise sea
w: Reachable only by a short taxi-boat from Vela Luka on Korcula's western tip, this uninhabited islet has no roads, no permanent structures and no fresh water, only pale limestone slabs sloping gently into water so clear the seabed stays visible many metres down. Locals have long called it the island of love.
why: One of the Adriatic's clearest, least-developed swimming spots, reachable only by boat and empty of any settlement.

s: Heated fjord-side saltwater pool by Bergen's aquarium
w: Opened in 1910 beside what is now Bergen's aquarium, this pool pipes in fjord water and warms it to a forgiving 30 degrees Celsius, with the colder open fjord itself just steps away for anyone wanting the real thing. Saunas keep the ritual going from June deep into winter.
why: A century-old saltwater institution letting Bergen swimmers choose between a heated pool and the open fjord.

s: Iceland's oldest pool, abandoned in a volcanic valley
w: Built by local youth groups in 1923 to teach fishermen's children to swim, this moss-walled pool sits alone in a mountain valley beneath Eyjafjallajokull, fed continuously by a hot spring. Long abandoned by its village, it draws hikers willing to walk twenty minutes for a soak with no facilities at all.
why: Built in 1923 as one of Iceland's first purpose-built swimming pools, still fed by a hot spring despite decades of abandonment.

s: A swimming pool built inside a hollowed river barge
w: The Spree is too polluted for a swim, so in 2004 an art collective sank a shipping barge's hull into it and filled the hollow with clean, filtered water, mooring the whole thing on the East Harbour bank. Sunbathers now lie on the barge's steel deck with the TV Tower and Oberbaum Bridge framing the skyline behind them.
why: An art project turned Berlin institution: a converted cargo barge pool floating on the too-polluted-to-swim-in Spree.

s: False Bay tidal pool refilled twice daily by the sea
w: Built into the rocks along the False Bay railway line, this tidal pool fills and empties with each tide, its low stone wall breaking the swell while letting cold Atlantic water flush through. Locals treat the pre-work dip as ritual, often followed by coffee at a cafe on the coastal path just above it.
why: One of Cape Town's best-loved tidal pools, cleaned and refreshed by the tide against a rocky False Bay shoreline.

s: Rainbow bathing huts guard False Bay's postcard pool
w: A row of Victorian-era bathing huts painted in candy stripes lines the sand above this rock-walled tidal pool between Muizenberg and Kalk Bay, making it one of the most photographed swimming spots on the peninsula. Shark spotters watch the bay while families paddle in the pool's sheltered, tide-fed water.
why: Cape Town's most photographed tidal pool, framed by Victorian-era beach huts painted in candy colours.

s: Blue wooden fishing boats crowd an Atlantic rampart port
w: Cannons still line the eighteenth-century Portuguese-built ramparts above this working Atlantic harbour, where blue wooden boats unload sardines each afternoon under a wheeling cloud of gulls. Fishermen mend nets by hand on the quay while grilled catch is sold straight from stalls a few steps from the water.
why: A working Atlantic fishing harbour ringed by centuries-old ramparts, its blue boats little changed in generations.

s: A honey-scented market threading canals of the Green Lung
w: Tucked inside Bang Kachao, an oxbow of jungle so close to Bangkok it is nicknamed the city's green lung, this canal-side market sells organic honey, fruit and noodles from wooden stalls rather than boats, reached by a five-minute cross-river ferry and a bicycle ride through mangrove and papaya groves.
why: The main market of Bang Kachao, a jungle river-bend so close to Bangkok it is nicknamed the city's Green Lung.

s: Mekong traders hang their wares from bamboo poles
w: Before dawn, small wooden boats converge on this quiet stretch of the Mekong Delta, each hanging a sample of its cargo from a tall bamboo pole so buyers can spot a seller from afar. Quieter than the crowded Cai Rang market downstream, it still runs on farmers' schedules, not tour buses.
why: A quieter, dawn-only alternative to Can Tho's famous Cai Rang market, still run by small-boat farmers rather than tour operators.

s: An open-air onsen where waves nearly reach the tub
w: Set directly on the shoreline rocks of Hokkawa Onsen on the Izu Peninsula's Pacific coast, this open-air hot spring puts bathers close enough to the sea that spray can reach the water's edge on a rough day. Separate stone and round tubs serve men and women, both open to nothing but sky and horizon.
why: A rare open-air hot spring set directly on the shoreline rocks, close enough that Pacific spray can reach the bathers.

s: River-edge hot baths bathing since the 1600s
w: Stone-lined baths sit right at the water's edge along the Kusu River in Kyushu, part of a riverside bathing tradition dating to the 1600s and unusual in Japan for having no walls or partitions between bathers and the passing current. Steam rises off the open Jinden-yu bath as the river runs by just beyond its rim.
why: One of Japan's rare riverside bathing traditions, with wall-less stone baths open to the river since the Edo period.

s: An 18th-century stepwell reborn as a diving spot
w: Commissioned in the 1740s by a royal queen as a public water source, this sandstone stepwell descends in galleries to a pool that fell into neglect for decades before a clean-up restored its water. Local boys now treat its stacked ledges as diving platforms, plunging past old stonework into the water below.
why: An 18th-century royal stepwell, once left to decay, now cleaned up and used by local boys for daredevil dives.

s: Cascading white terraces of mineral-warm bathing pools
w: Calcite-laden thermal water has spent millennia crusting this hillside in blinding white travertine, spilling through terraced pools that Greeks and Romans revered as a sacred gateway when they built Hierapolis above it. Bathers wade barefoot across the mineral crust between step-like basins of warm water.
why: A UNESCO-listed cascade of calcium-white terraces that Greeks and Romans already revered as sacred bathing pools two millennia ago.

s: A cliff-foot ocean pool with a lonely, wave-battered feel
w: A steep path drops down a cliff face on the New South Wales Sapphire Coast to reach this rock-cut ocean pool, cold Tasman swell washing straight through a low seaward wall. Fewer crowds and no facilities keep it a cult favourite among ocean-pool hunters willing to make the climb back up afterward.
why: A cult favourite among ocean-pool hunters, set at the base of a dramatic cliff on the NSW Sapphire Coast.

s: A secluded rock-platform pool below the escarpment
w: A wide rock platform at the south end of Coledale Beach shelters this ocean pool beneath the green wall of the Illawarra escarpment, one of dozens strung along a coast holding roughly half the world's ocean pools. Fewer visitors reach it than the better-known pools closer to Sydney, leaving it secluded most mornings.
why: One of the Illawarra coast's least crowded ocean pools, reached across a wide tidal rock shelf south of Sydney.

s: Indian Ocean swell foams through a granite jacuzzi
w: Southern Ocean swell forces its way through a narrow gap in granite boulders near Injidup Beach, whipping the trapped water into a frothing natural jacuzzi before it settles into a clear rock pool below. Margaret River wine country lies just inland, but this basin belongs entirely to the wind and the swell.
why: A wave-carved granite basin where Indian Ocean swell forces through narrow gaps to whip the water into natural jacuzzi foam.

s: Dig your own thermal spa in the sand at low tide
w: Two hours either side of low tide, geothermal water rising through the sand here turns the beach into a communal dig site, with visitors hollowing out personal hot pools using nothing more than a rented spade. The Pacific surf sits metres away, cold enough to shock anyone who steps out of their self-made spa too fast.
why: A geothermal beach where anyone with a spade can dig their own private hot pool in the sand between the tides.

s: Ruined foundations of the world's largest bathhouse
w: Opened in 1896 with six saltwater pools and one freshwater pool under a vast glass roof, this was once the largest indoor swimming establishment on earth, holding close to two million gallons at Lands End. Fire gutted the structure in 1966, leaving concrete foundations that flood and drain with the Pacific tide.
why: Once the world's largest indoor swimming complex, now a haunting set of concrete ruins battered by the Pacific.

s: North America's longest outdoor pool, tide-fed and heated
w: Opened in 1931 and billed at the time as America's largest swimming pool, this 137-metre saltwater pool still pumps water straight from English Bay and heats it for three-season comfort. A 2018 upgrade cut its fresh water use by eighty percent while keeping the tide-replenished saltwater tradition intact.
why: At 137 metres, the longest outdoor pool in North America, filled with heated saltwater pumped straight from English Bay.

s: A jungle sinkhole beside forgotten Mayan pyramids
w: A short bike ride through jungle from the little-visited Ek Balam pyramids leads to this open limestone sinkhole, its cool turquoise water ringed by hanging roots and a wooden platform for jumping in. Far fewer crowds reach it than the cenotes near Tulum, leaving the ruins-and-swim combination refreshingly quiet.
why: A quieter alternative to Yucatan's crowded cenotes, reached by bike through jungle beside the little-visited Ek Balam ruins.

s: Sunbeams turn a cave sinkhole electric blue at noon
w: Sunlight angling through a narrow opening in this limestone cave, deep in Bahia's Chapada Diamantina, hits suspended particles and turns the chamber an almost unreal, glowing blue around midday. Unlike its more famous, swim-banned neighbour Poco Encantado, snorkellers are welcome to drift through the clear water.
why: A flooded limestone cave where midday sun through a rock opening turns the clear water an intense, glowing blue for snorkellers.

s: A WPA-era giant pool shadowed by two East River bridges
w: Built in 1936 under Robert Moses's WPA pool program, this Olympic-scale outdoor pool sits in Astoria Park directly beneath the steel arcs of the Hell Gate and Triborough bridges. It was briefly the largest pool in New York City at opening and remains one of the most dramatically sited of the era's surviving pools.
why: One of the largest and oldest of New York's WPA-era pools, built in 1936 beneath the Hell Gate and Triborough bridges.

s: A working cove harbour under Valparaiso's painted hills
w: Small wooden fishing boats crowd this sheltered cove beneath Valparaiso's tumbling, graffiti-bright hillside barrios, with a daily catch of conger eel and shellfish sold off the boats and cooked at plastic-table cocinerias steps from the water. Pelicans and sea lions loiter for scraps as the boats come in each morning.
why: A working fishermen's cove tucked beneath Valparaiso's colourful hillside barrios, its catch sold straight off the boats each morning.
